sources.title: Trump says there are ways to 'rein' in AI 'if we have to' - Yahoo
passages: "We will be careful, and that's why we have the Department of Justice, and other Law Enforcement bodies, that will rein things in if we have to," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
President Donald Trump suggested there are existing ways to "rein" in AI.
In the US, states including California and Illinois have led AI regulation efforts as Congress has struggled to reach consensus.
Trump has issued multiple AI-related executive actions, but there are limits to what he can do.
One potential regulatory area could center around liability.
Earlier Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration would not grant frontier AI labs protection from such risks.
Trump and his administration are being closely watched to see how they respond to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's renewed push for federal regulation.
After Amodei renewed his request, Trump and Vice President JD Vance both expressed skepticism that AI companies would ask the government to impose regulations that would slow parts of the industry.

In his post on Monday, Trump reiterated his view that the current conversation around AI safety is a "hoax" akin to his stated opinions on climate change, questions about his 2016 campaign's relationship with Russia, and the circumstances of his first impeachment.

A federal judge in Rhode Island has struck down a Trump administration directive that would have barred some immigrants from accessing certain federal programs, including Head Start preschools, community health clinics and adult education programs.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a preference to use a light touch when it comes to AI regulation.
Previously, Trump suggested that the only guardrail the US needed was himself because he was smart enough to know how to manage the technology.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said Monday that the Department of Justice and other U.S. law enforcement agencies will rein in risks associated with artificial intelligence "if we have to." "We will be careful," Trump said in a Truth Social post. Trump's mention of the DOJ as a backstop came as he again downplayed potential dangers from AI , which he has repeatedly called a hoax in the past two weeks, after Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher at Anthropic , quit his job and warned that that company and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives" with the technology. The president has touted AI development by American companies as a competitive advantage for the United States, which he wants to maintain. "Whoever wins AI, WINS!" Trump wrote in his post. "We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I'm going to keep it that way!" he wrote. "I'm not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself." "We will be careful, and that's why we have the Department of Justice, and other Law Enforcement bodies, that will rein things in if we have to, but I will only encourage AI or, SI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)!" Trump wrote. The president, in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post, wrote, "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies." Since Coxon's warning, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind, have called for a slowdown of AI development and extra federal oversight of their industry. The White House has largely taken a light approach to AI regulation, with Trump's executive order in June laying out a loose plan for review. That order asked companies to voluntarily work with the administration to evaluate "covered frontier models" and give the government access up to 30 days before a broad release. extraction.body: Seattle Met 329 NE Couch Street, Suite 200 Portland, OR 97232 By Grace Madigan August 31, 2026 Published in the Fall 2026 issue of Seattle Met On Wednesday, September 2, bells will ring for more than 40,000 students to signal the first day of school at Seattle Public Schools (unless a teacher strike intervenes). But phones will not. Last spring, superintendent Ben Shuldiner announced no-phone policies for grades K-12; they went into effect May 4, his 100th day in office. extraction.body: Summary: Seattle Public Schools is updating how technology is used in kindergarten through second grade classrooms beginning Jan. 4, 2027. Seattle Public Schools is updating how technology is used in kindergarten through second grade classrooms beginning Jan. 4, 2027. As part of this shift, SPS will move away from the current 1:1 iPad model, in which each kindergarten through second grade student is assigned their own individual iPad for usage at school or home, and transition to a classroom-based approach to technology access in grades K-2. iPads will remain available at school, and teachers will use them intentionally when technology supports instruction, accessibility, assessment, or other approved learning activities. Students in kindergarten through second grade will have limited daily technology use, generally ranging from 0 to 30 minutes as part of a balanced instructional day. This does not mean students will be required to use technology every day. Some days may include no iPad use when the learning goal is better supported through direct instruction, reading, writing, discussion, manipulatives, movement, or hands-on exploration. Technology will continue to be one of many tools teachers use to support student learning. Our focus is to ensure technology complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on, social, language-rich, and interpersonal experiences that are especially important during the early elementary years. District-adopted curriculum and instructional resources include technology components, and students will continue to engage with those tools when they are part of classroom learning. Teachers will use technology intentionally and in developmentally appropriate ways alongside direct instruction and other classroom experiences. What is changing? Beginning Jan. 4, 2027, K-2 students will no longer be assigned an individual iPad through the 1:1 device model. Instead, iPads will be shared and managed as classroom resources. How much technology will students use? Daily technology use will generally range from 0 to 30 minutes. The amount of time may vary based on the lesson and student needs, and technology will not be required every day. Will students still use iPads? Yes. iPads will remain available in classrooms for approved learning activities, assessments, accessibility supports, and other situations in which technology meaningfully supports instruction. What will learning look like without individual devices? Students will continue to learn through teacher-led instruction, reading, writing, discussion, small-group work, hands-on activities, manipulatives, movement, creative projects, and exploration. Technology will be used when it adds value to these experiences. What about district-adopted curriculum? Students will continue to use the technology components included in district-adopted curriculum and instructional resources when those tools are part of classroom learning. What about students who need technology for accessibility or other supports? Technology will remain available when needed for accessibility, assessment, approved instructional activities, or other student supports. Additional implementation guidance will be shared as details are finalized. This change reflects our continued focus on providing developmentally appropriate learning experiences for our youngest students while ensuring technology remains available when it meaningfully supports learning. Additional details and family resources will be shared before the change takes effect. If you have questions, please contact Seattle Public Schools using Let’s Talk. Thank you for your continued support of our students and schools. extraction.body: Summary: Seattle Public Schools is updating how technology is used in kindergarten through second grade classrooms beginning Jan. 4, 2027. Seattle Public Schools is updating how technology is used in kindergarten through second grade classrooms beginning Jan. 4, 2027. As part of this shift, SPS will move away from the current 1:1 iPad model, in which each kindergarten through second grade student is assigned their own individual iPad for usage at school or home, and transition to a classroom-based approach to technology access in grades K-2. iPads will remain available at school, and teachers will use them intentionally when technology supports instruction, accessibility, assessment, or other approved learning activities. Students in kindergarten through second grade will have limited daily technology use, generally ranging from 0 to 30 minutes as part of a balanced instructional day. This does not mean students will be required to use technology every day. Some days may include no iPad use when the learning goal is better supported through direct instruction, reading, writing, discussion, manipulatives, movement, or hands-on exploration. Technology will continue to be one of many tools teachers use to support student learning. Our focus is to ensure technology complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on, social, language-rich, and interpersonal experiences that are especially important during the early elementary years. District-adopted curriculum and instructional resources include technology components, and students will continue to engage with those tools when they are part of classroom learning. Teachers will use technology intentionally and in developmentally appropriate ways alongside direct instruction and other classroom experiences. What is changing? Beginning Jan. 4, 2027, K-2 students will no longer be assigned an individual iPad through the 1:1 device model. Instead, iPads will be shared and managed as classroom resources. How much technology will students use? Daily technology use will generally range from 0 to 30 minutes. The amount of time may vary based on the lesson and student needs, and technology will not be required every day. Will students still use iPads? Yes. iPads will remain available in classrooms for approved learning activities, assessments, accessibility supports, and other situations in which technology meaningfully supports instruction. What will learning look like without individual devices? Students will continue to learn through teacher-led instruction, reading, writing, discussion, small-group work, hands-on activities, manipulatives, movement, creative projects, and exploration. Technology will be used when it adds value to these experiences. What about district-adopted curriculum? Students will continue to use the technology components included in district-adopted curriculum and instructional resources when those tools are part of classroom learning. What about students who need technology for accessibility or other supports? Technology will remain available when needed for accessibility, assessment, approved instructional activities, or other student supports. Additional implementation guidance will be shared as details are finalized. This change reflects our continued focus on providing developmentally appropriate learning experiences for our youngest students while ensuring technology remains available when it meaningfully supports learning. Additional details and family resources will be shared before the change takes effect. If you have questions, please contact Seattle Public Schools using Let’s Talk. Thank you for your continued support of our students and schools. passages: Finding the best crypto to buy now is on the radar of many investors as crypto markets are at an inflection point in September 2026.

Bitcoin has consolidated below its all-time high, yet institutional inflows via ETFs remain structurally positive, and Ethereum’s Pectra and Glamsterdam upgrades are actively reshaping its throughput.
The markets are beginning to pick up with capital inflowing into the sector.
For investors entering now, the key question isn’t whether to buy crypto; it’s which assets match your time horizon and risk appetite.
September 2026 has seen an impressive crypto rally with Bitcoin leading the charge.
Bitcoin has shot from $60,000 to $85,000 in just two weeks.

Bitcoin has plenty of momentum, is leading the crypto charge, and we are seeing Bitcoin ETF inflows in the positive, leading investors to expect Bitcoin still has some room to run and possibly reclaim the coveted $100,000 price point.
XRP has one of the strongest and most loyal fan bases in all of crypto, and with the September 2026, the “XRP Army” is in full force, propelling the asset over 10% in just 7 days.
It behaves like a decentralized, highly profitable financial institution.

Rather than relying on predatory unlocks or inflationary token subsidies, the custom Layer 1 commands dominant market share in perpetual derivatives while channeling massive fee revenue straight into continuous programmatic buybacks.
Solana SOL +2.20% is a very fast blockchain, handling around 960 transactions per second as of September 2026, with almost no fees, even when many people use it at once.
Its built-in time-stamping system helps it stay quick and smooth, making it a favorite for DeFi apps, NFTs, and busy trading platforms.
As memecoins continue to outperform many other crypto projects, Dogecoin is the most recognized “blue chip” memecoin that ends up taking most of the liquidity.
If you want to invest in established crypto projects (a.k.a. dino coins ), look at their past price charts and how they handled tough periods, such as the 2022–2023 crypto winter.
Cardano has chosen a different route than the path followed by Ethereum and Solana.
Cardano is a research-focused blockchain led by a highly technical team that prioritizes compliance and technological accuracy over speed and marketing.
This is evident in Cardano’s 100% uptime and interest expressed by governments and academic institutions.
There’s no one “best” crypto for a $1,000 investment.
Conservative investors consider Bitcoin or Ethereum as core long‑term holdings, while growth-oriented investors prefer smaller‑cap tokens for their upside potential despite the higher risk.
Ethereum is mid-cycle in a meaningful upgrade sequence.
Pectra (live since May 2026) already increased validator staking limits and improved wallet UX.
The Glamsterdam fork , targeting mid-2026, is designed to push transaction capacity well beyond its current ceiling.
What this means practically: fees get cheaper, the network handles more traffic, and Ethereum becomes a more credible rails layer for stablecoins and tokenized assets.
ETH staking yields currently sit around 3–4% annually, which adds a carry component most blue chips can’t offer.
Solana is the leading Ethereum competitor and has completely dominated the memecoin narrative.
Projects needing fast transactions and instant settlements favour Solana, which has been seen with SOL’s performance skyrocketing 30% during the September market rally.
Solana also has multiple ETFs available for institutional investors, which have also been supporting the rally.

Active in the industry since 2023, she first became fascinated...
The Voltaire governance era handed on-chain control to ADA holders, a structural first for a major L1.
Hydra (layer-2 scalability) is moving from testnet to more active deployment, and Midnight, the privacy sidechain, is targeting regulated finance use cases where confidentiality is non-negotiable.
For investors, the staking yield (currently ~3% annualized) provides an income floor while waiting for ecosystem growth to materialize.
Ethereum is a consistent market leader and the leading layer 1, forming the foundation of DeFi, DePin, and much of the crypto infrastructure.
Ethereum is expected to continue to perform well as profits rotate out of Bitcoin and find its way into the Ethereum ecosystem.
It is all about reliability and speed in the Solana 2026 story.
Firedancer introduces a second validator client, eliminating the risk of cutover, and pushing higher throughput.
Alpenglow is seeking higher finality and reduced latency.
As the compute limits become larger and the token transfers reduce in cost, the fees decline.
The latter combination facilitates the operation of DeFi, gaming, and meme trading.

For 2026, many analysts point to Bitcoin for its liquidity and macro hedge appeal, but Ethereum gets cited more often as having the most overall potential due to network activity, developer ecosystem, smart contract dominance, and upcoming upgrades.
Meme coins like Dogecoin and Pepe also rank among the most actively traded tokens.
The best long-term crypto assets represent large markets with millions of users and high trading volumes.
Historically, crypto assets, particularly Bitcoin and Ethereum, have benefited when liquidity conditions improve.
Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP are established ecosystems with entire markets built around them.
Not exactly, Bitcoin is the first and most well-known cryptocurrency, but the term “crypto” refers to the entire category of digital assets, including Ethereum, Solana, and other altcoins.
The most popular cryptocurrencies have a large market cap and many users, for example, Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), BNB (BNB), XRP (XRP), and Solana (SOL).

The bullish rebound comes following comments Wednesday from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who declined to say whether the agency planned rate hikes later this year. On Thursday, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that employers reported adding significantly fewer jobs in June than expected—57,000 vs. a target of 115,000, down from a revised figure of 129,000 jobs added in May. passages: The “Horowitz Andreessen Academy” will launch with 10 partners, including Anduril, Anthropic, Coinbase, Google, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit, and Stripe, along with $42 million in funding led by a16z.
Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) is creating an “academy” positioned as a pipeline for young people to build or join a Silicon Valley startup.

The announcement says they’ll have “no traditional grades, tests, or homework,” but will “learn from Silicon Valley’s most storied founders and operators in short, high-impact classes and spend the rest of your time working and exploring.” The academy seems like the latest attempt by Silicon Valley’s billionaires to “fix” America’s education system by creating their own.
Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos have all poured money into starting their own schools, while a16z founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz have been critical of colleges.

extraction.body: Andreessen Horowitz has launched the Horowitz Andreessen Academy — a highly selective San Francisco school positioned as a college alternative. No grades, no tuition for the founding class, and Sam Altman on the faculty. Andreessen Horowitz, popularly known by their monicker a16z, has spent nearly two decades in identifying, and investing in some of the most disruptive companies of this generation. The legendary investor is now looking to create “AI-native” talent for some of these promising companies, as it launches the Horowitz Andreessen Academy , a highly selective school that positions itself as a direct alternative to your classic four year college degree. Applications are open for the Founding Class Fellowship, a one-year programme starting Fall 2027. It is tuition-free, and includes travel and everything else to start with. Everything after that — a two-year programme the Academy intends to launch in Fall 2028, pending regulatory approval — will cost roughly what an elite private university does. The Academy has raised $42M in funding, led by a16z, with Marc Andreessen and Erik Torenberg on the board. Angels include Tobi Lütke, Garry Tan, Tony Xu, and Adam D’Angelo. It also has ten founding partners, which includes the likes of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Nvidia among others. Gagan Biyani, the founder of Udemy & Maven, and the one leading this Horowitz Andreessen Academy said, “The focus of The Academy is on building – which we believe is the most valuable thing humans can do to learn to become a productive, curious and happy adult. Our goal is to help high school graduates thrive by cultivating this instinct. Building is an underlying skill that helps you create lifelong friendships, be indispensable at work, create jobs by providing value to society, and discover your inner joy. That’s why we’re doing this”. The Academy is structured around three things: Pursuits, Courses, and Co-ops. Pursuits are personal projects — startup ideas, rabbit holes, quests — that students choose themselves. Courses are short, high-impact programmes — anywhere from two days to four weeks — taught by actual practitioners. And Co-ops are immersive stints at real companies. The Academy launches with ten founding partners — Anduril, Anthropic, Coinbase, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit, and Stripe — who will co-create curriculum, provide compute access, and offer hands-on learning opportunities. Founding Class Fellows receive $50,000 in compute credits, a $5,000 travel and research budget, and no tuition bill. There are no grades, no tests, and no homework. The Academy is located in the heart of San Francisco. Applications are officially open for the Founding Class Fellowship, the academy’s inaugural one-year program, which will begin in Fall of 2027. Notably, Founding Class Fellowship will be tuition-free. The Tech Portal is published by Blue Box Media Private Limited . Our investors have no influence over our reporting. The announcement says they’ll have “no traditional grades, tests, or homework,” but will “learn from Silicon Valley’s most storied founders and operators in short, high-impact classes and spend the rest of your time working and exploring.” The academy seems like the latest attempt by Silicon Valley’s billionaires to “fix” America’s education system by creating their own. extraction.body: Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) is creating an “academy” positioned as a pipeline for young people to build or join a Silicon Valley startup. The “Horowitz Andreessen Academy” will launch with 10 partners, including Anduril, Anthropic, Coinbase, Google, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit, and Stripe, along with $42 million in funding led by a16z. While billed as a “highly selective school,” it does not grant any degree or accreditation. Instead, students will attend short classes led by tech figureheads, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, as well as “co-ops” that give students roles at tech companies. To partake in the one-year program, students will have to move to San Francisco and arrange their own housing, according to the academy’s FAQ page. Students are promised more than $50,000 in compute credits and a $5,000 travel and research budget offered by a16z. The announcement says they’ll have “no traditional grades, tests, or homework,” but will “learn from Silicon Valley’s most storied founders and operators in short, high-impact classes and spend the rest of your time working and exploring.” The academy seems like the latest attempt by Silicon Valley’s billionaires to “fix” America’s education system by creating their own. Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos have all poured money into starting their own schools, while a16z founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz have been critical of colleges. Last year, Andreessen reportedly called Stanford and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology “political lobbying operations fighting American innovation” in a group chat with White House officials and tech leaders, according to The Washington Post. The Horowitz Andreessen Academy will be free for its first one-year program in the fall of 2027. It will only accept 50 students and is designed mainly for recent high school graduates.

extraction.body: Andreessen Horowitz has launched the Horowitz Andreessen Academy — a highly selective San Francisco school positioned as a college alternative. No grades, no tuition for the founding class, and Sam Altman on the faculty. Andreessen Horowitz, popularly known by their monicker a16z, has spent nearly two decades in identifying, and investing in some of the most disruptive companies of this generation. The legendary investor is now looking to create “AI-native” talent for some of these promising companies, as it launches the Horowitz Andreessen Academy , a highly selective school that positions itself as a direct alternative to your classic four year college degree. Applications are open for the Founding Class Fellowship, a one-year programme starting Fall 2027. It is tuition-free, and includes travel and everything else to start with. Everything after that — a two-year programme the Academy intends to launch in Fall 2028, pending regulatory approval — will cost roughly what an elite private university does. The Academy has raised $42M in funding, led by a16z, with Marc Andreessen and Erik Torenberg on the board. Angels include Tobi Lütke, Garry Tan, Tony Xu, and Adam D’Angelo. It also has ten founding partners, which includes the likes of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Nvidia among others. Gagan Biyani, the founder of Udemy & Maven, and the one leading this Horowitz Andreessen Academy said, “The focus of The Academy is on building – which we believe is the most valuable thing humans can do to learn to become a productive, curious and happy adult. Our goal is to help high school graduates thrive by cultivating this instinct. Building is an underlying skill that helps you create lifelong friendships, be indispensable at work, create jobs by providing value to society, and discover your inner joy. That’s why we’re doing this”. The Academy is structured around three things: Pursuits, Courses, and Co-ops. Pursuits are personal projects — startup ideas, rabbit holes, quests — that students choose themselves. Courses are short, high-impact programmes — anywhere from two days to four weeks — taught by actual practitioners. And Co-ops are immersive stints at real companies. The Academy launches with ten founding partners — Anduril, Anthropic, Coinbase, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit, and Stripe — who will co-create curriculum, provide compute access, and offer hands-on learning opportunities. Founding Class Fellows receive $50,000 in compute credits, a $5,000 travel and research budget, and no tuition bill. There are no grades, no tests, and no homework. The Academy is located in the heart of San Francisco. Applications are officially open for the Founding Class Fellowship, the academy’s inaugural one-year program, which will begin in Fall of 2027. Notably, Founding Class Fellowship will be tuition-free. The Tech Portal is published by Blue Box Media Private Limited . Our investors have no influence over our reporting. Read our full Ownership and Funding Disclosure → Surabhi is a technology journalist with a focus on Startups, Emerging technology and daily tech briefs globally. She is based in Bengaluru.

passages: But resources like that aren’t available to startups, so AstroForge , which is developing technology to mine asteroids, is turning to AI.
The company has developed an autonomous control stack for its spacecraft called “Solo,” a transformer-based model made in-house.

AstroForge, founded in 2022 and backed with $56 million in venture funding, has launched two prototype spacecraft, both of which suffered anomalies that prevented them from achieving most of their mission objectives.
In 2025, its Odin spacecraft was launched into deep space, but the company had difficulty communicating with it.
There are a limited number of antennas on Earth big enough to transmit to spacecraft hundreds of thousands of miles away, and the windows of time in which to do it are small.
“Would that have been recoverable with all the data on the spacecraft?

I don’t know, but I can tell you nothing onboard tried it, and I would love something onboard to try if the spacecraft is unrecoverable at launch,” Matthew Gialich, AstroForge’s co-founder and CEO, said.

It created a stack that includes traditional control algorithms, models trained on test data for specific subsystems like power generation or navigation, and an overall intelligence layer trained on about 2,500 sensors in the spacecraft.
AstroForge plans to fly its first autonomous spacecraft in 2027 on the first rocket launched by Stoke Space.
That mission will be backed by NASA and is expected to gather scientific data about the sun.
The company’s third vehicle, DeepSpace-2, is currently set to launch alongside Intuitive Machines’ third moon mission, expected to head for space by the end of 2026.

extraction.body: Fly to an asteroid, land on it, make no mistakes: If only it were that easy. When NASA sends spacecraft to explore the solar system, they build in redundancy and automation. But much of the work is done by teams of flight controllers communicating with the vehicle from Earth. The OSIRIS-REx mission, which rendezvoused with an asteroid in 2018, had 100 operators on each eight-hour shift. But resources like that aren’t available to startups, so AstroForge , which is developing technology to mine asteroids, is turning to AI. The company has developed an autonomous control stack for its spacecraft called “Solo,” a transformer-based model made in-house. AstroForge plans to fly its first autonomous spacecraft in 2027 on the first rocket launched by Stoke Space. That mission will be backed by NASA and is expected to gather scientific data about the sun. That would be an accomplishment: Most spacecraft autonomy depends on traditional control algorithms due to concerns about the unreliability of neural networks. The first use of a neural network to control a satellite’s positioning in orbit took place just last year . AstroForge, founded in 2022 and backed with $56 million in venture funding, has launched two prototype spacecraft, both of which suffered anomalies that prevented them from achieving most of their mission objectives. In 2025, its Odin spacecraft was launched into deep space, but the company had difficulty communicating with it. There are a limited number of antennas on Earth big enough to transmit to spacecraft hundreds of thousands of miles away, and the windows of time in which to do it are small. Ultimately, AstroForge couldn’t gain control of Odin, but the experience spurred it to consider alternatives: Could it put sufficient intelligence onboard the spacecraft for it to solve its own problems? “Would that have been recoverable with all the data on the spacecraft? I don’t know, but I can tell you nothing onboard tried it, and I would love something onboard to try if the spacecraft is unrecoverable at launch,” Matthew Gialich, AstroForge’s co-founder and CEO, said. “The trade for me is: Do I go build my own ground network, which is going to cost [around] $200 million to put up five dishes around the world and then do operations on it, or do I try to remove it with a model?” Armand Awad, AstroForge’s head of flight software, said the company decided to leverage the advances in transformer models driven by the frontier labs. It created a stack that includes traditional control algorithms, models trained on test data for specific subsystems like power generation or navigation, and an overall intelligence layer trained on about 2,500 sensors in the spacecraft. “I’m not saying I’m going to make general spacecraft autonomy or general autonomy for the world,” Gialich said. “I’m making a constrained autonomy at a very low sensor input, following the basic training of a transformer model.” In theory, the agent in control of the spacecraft will perform tasks like anomaly resolution. Awad imagines it realizing that it has lost track of its position in space, correlating a power anomaly to issues in its star tracker, and fixing the whole thing — “probably turning it on and off in this case.” The company’s third vehicle, DeepSpace-2, is currently set to launch alongside Intuitive Machines’ third moon mission, expected to head for space by the end of 2026. Solo will be onboard that vehicle, flying in “shadow mode,” so AstroForge’s engineers can put it through its paces before the Autonomy-1 mission. Will this truly be an AI agent operating an independent spacecraft? “I don’t plan on flying radios that can receive from Earth on Autonomy-1,” Gialich said. “We have to go all in right now. The team’s probably going to talk me into it by the time we fly it. sources.title: AstroForge Puts AI in Command of Next Spacecraft Mission
passages: Space mining startup AstroForge is making a bold leap into AI-powered space exploration with Autonomy-1, their next spacecraft that will operate under the command of a compact transformer-based AI model.
AstroForge's decision to entrust spacecraft command to AI represents more than just a technological upgrade - it's a fundamental shift toward truly autonomous space exploration.

Traditional spacecraft rely on pre-programmed sequences and basic rule-based systems, but AstroForge is betting that transformer models - the same architecture powering ChatGPT and other large language models - can handle the complex decision-making required for asteroid mining operations.

AstroForge will need to demonstrate that their compressed AI model can maintain reliability in the harsh radiation environment of space while making split-second decisions that could determine mission success or failure.
Most spacecraft today operate on relatively simple command sequences uploaded from Earth, with limited ability to adapt to unexpected situations.
The implications extend far beyond AstroForge's immediate mission goals.
What makes this particularly intriguing is the potential for AI spacecraft to learn and adapt during their missions.
The success of this mission won't just validate AstroForge's approach; it could establish the template for how humanity explores the solar system in the decades ahead.

The move represents one of the first commercial deployments of modern AI architecture in deep space operations, potentially reshaping how we approach autonomous space missions when human oversight isn't practical. AstroForge just announced a game-changing approach to space exploration that could redefine how we operate beyond Earth's orbit. The space mining startup revealed that their upcoming Autonomy-1 mission will be commanded by a small but sophisticated transformer-based AI model, marking what appears to be the first commercial deployment of modern AI architecture in deep space operations. When you're operating millions of miles from Earth, the communication delays make real-time human control impossible. Traditional spacecraft rely on pre-programmed sequences and basic rule-based systems, but AstroForge is betting that transformer models - the same architecture powering ChatGPT and other large language models - can handle the complex decision-making required for asteroid mining operations. This represents a massive technical leap from current space operations. Most spacecraft today operate on relatively simple command sequences uploaded from Earth, with limited ability to adapt to unexpected situations. The transformer model aboard Autonomy-1 will need to process sensor data, make navigation decisions, and potentially identify valuable asteroid targets without waiting for instructions from mission control. The implications extend far beyond AstroForge's immediate mission goals. If successful, this approach could establish a new paradigm for deep space exploration, where AI-powered spacecraft operate as truly autonomous agents rather than remote-controlled robots. NASA and other space agencies have been experimenting with AI in space for years, but mostly in supporting roles rather than primary command functions. Transformer models typically require significant computational resources, but spacecraft operate under strict power and processing constraints. AstroForge will need to demonstrate that their compressed AI model can maintain reliability in the harsh radiation environment of space while making split-second decisions that could determine mission success or failure. For the broader space industry, Autonomy-1 could signal the beginning of a new era where AI becomes the standard approach for deep space missions. Companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin have focused primarily on launch capabilities and near-Earth operations, but autonomous AI could be the key to unlocking more ambitious missions to asteroids, Mars, and beyond. The timing aligns with growing investor interest in space technology and AI applications. AstroForge has positioned itself at the intersection of two of the hottest tech sectors, potentially creating a blueprint that other space startups will rush to follow. The success or failure of Autonomy-1 won't just determine the company's future - it could influence how the entire industry approaches autonomous space operations. What makes this particularly intriguing is the potential for AI spacecraft to learn and adapt during their missions. Unlike traditional systems that operate within fixed parameters, transformer-based models could theoretically improve their performance as they encounter new situations, making each subsequent mission more capable than the last. AstroForge's decision to entrust spacecraft command to AI represents more than just a technological upgrade - it's a fundamental shift toward truly autonomous space exploration. If Autonomy-1 succeeds, we could be looking at the dawn of an era where AI-powered spacecraft operate as independent explorers, making discoveries and decisions millions of miles from human oversight. The success of this mission won't just validate AstroForge's approach; it could establish the template for how humanity explores the solar system in the decades ahead.

extraction.body: Fly to an asteroid, land on it, make no mistakes: If only it were that easy. When NASA sends spacecraft to explore the solar system, they build in redundancy and automation. But much of the work is done by teams of flight controllers communicating with the vehicle from Earth. The OSIRIS-REx mission, which rendezvoused with an asteroid in 2018, had 100 operators on each eight-hour shift. But resources like that aren’t available to startups, so AstroForge , which is developing technology to mine asteroids, is turning to AI. The company has developed an autonomous control stack for its spacecraft called “Solo,” a transformer-based model made in-house. AstroForge plans to fly its first autonomous spacecraft in 2027 on the first rocket launched by Stoke Space. That mission will be backed by NASA and is expected to gather scientific data about the sun. That would be an accomplishment: Most spacecraft autonomy depends on traditional control algorithms due to concerns about the unreliability of neural networks. The first use of a neural network to control a satellite’s positioning in orbit took place just last year . AstroForge, founded in 2022 and backed with $56 million in venture funding, has launched two prototype spacecraft, both of which suffered anomalies that prevented them from achieving most of their mission objectives. In 2025, its Odin spacecraft was launched into deep space, but the company had difficulty communicating with it. There are a limited number of antennas on Earth big enough to transmit to spacecraft hundreds of thousands of miles away, and the windows of time in which to do it are small. Ultimately, AstroForge couldn’t gain control of Odin, but the experience spurred it to consider alternatives: Could it put sufficient intelligence onboard the spacecraft for it to solve its own problems? “Would that have been recoverable with all the data on the spacecraft? I don’t know, but I can tell you nothing onboard tried it, and I would love something onboard to try if the spacecraft is unrecoverable at launch,” Matthew Gialich, AstroForge’s co-founder and CEO, said. “The trade for me is: Do I go build my own ground network, which is going to cost [around] $200 million to put up five dishes around the world and then do operations on it, or do I try to remove it with a model?” Armand Awad, AstroForge’s head of flight software, said the company decided to leverage the advances in transformer models driven by the frontier labs. It created a stack that includes traditional control algorithms, models trained on test data for specific subsystems like power generation or navigation, and an overall intelligence layer trained on about 2,500 sensors in the spacecraft. “I’m not saying I’m going to make general spacecraft autonomy or general autonomy for the world,” Gialich said. “I’m making a constrained autonomy at a very low sensor input, following the basic training of a transformer model.” In theory, the agent in control of the spacecraft will perform tasks like anomaly resolution. Awad imagines it realizing that it has lost track of its position in space, correlating a power anomaly to issues in its star tracker, and fixing the whole thing — “probably turning it on and off in this case.” The company’s third vehicle, DeepSpace-2, is currently set to launch alongside Intuitive Machines’ third moon mission, expected to head for space by the end of 2026. Solo will be onboard that vehicle, flying in “shadow mode,” so AstroForge’s engineers can put it through its paces before the Autonomy-1 mission. Will this truly be an AI agent operating an independent spacecraft? “I don’t plan on flying radios that can receive from Earth on Autonomy-1,” Gialich said. “We have to go all in right now. The team’s probably going to talk me into it by the time we fly it. extraction.body: Space mining startup AstroForge is making a bold leap into AI-powered space exploration with Autonomy-1, their next spacecraft that will operate under the command of a compact transformer-based AI model. The move represents one of the first commercial deployments of modern AI architecture in deep space operations, potentially reshaping how we approach autonomous space missions when human oversight isn't practical. AstroForge just announced a game-changing approach to space exploration that could redefine how we operate beyond Earth's orbit. The space mining startup revealed that their upcoming Autonomy-1 mission will be commanded by a small but sophisticated transformer-based AI model, marking what appears to be the first commercial deployment of modern AI architecture in deep space operations. When you're operating millions of miles from Earth, the communication delays make real-time human control impossible. Traditional spacecraft rely on pre-programmed sequences and basic rule-based systems, but AstroForge is betting that transformer models - the same architecture powering ChatGPT and other large language models - can handle the complex decision-making required for asteroid mining operations. This represents a massive technical leap from current space operations. Most spacecraft today operate on relatively simple command sequences uploaded from Earth, with limited ability to adapt to unexpected situations. The transformer model aboard Autonomy-1 will need to process sensor data, make navigation decisions, and potentially identify valuable asteroid targets without waiting for instructions from mission control. The implications extend far beyond AstroForge's immediate mission goals. If successful, this approach could establish a new paradigm for deep space exploration, where AI-powered spacecraft operate as truly autonomous agents rather than remote-controlled robots. NASA and other space agencies have been experimenting with AI in space for years, but mostly in supporting roles rather than primary command functions. Transformer models typically require significant computational resources, but spacecraft operate under strict power and processing constraints. AstroForge will need to demonstrate that their compressed AI model can maintain reliability in the harsh radiation environment of space while making split-second decisions that could determine mission success or failure. For the broader space industry, Autonomy-1 could signal the beginning of a new era where AI becomes the standard approach for deep space missions. Companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin have focused primarily on launch capabilities and near-Earth operations, but autonomous AI could be the key to unlocking more ambitious missions to asteroids, Mars, and beyond. The timing aligns with growing investor interest in space technology and AI applications. AstroForge has positioned itself at the intersection of two of the hottest tech sectors, potentially creating a blueprint that other space startups will rush to follow. The success or failure of Autonomy-1 won't just determine the company's future - it could influence how the entire industry approaches autonomous space operations. What makes this particularly intriguing is the potential for AI spacecraft to learn and adapt during their missions. Unlike traditional systems that operate within fixed parameters, transformer-based models could theoretically improve their performance as they encounter new situations, making each subsequent mission more capable than the last. AstroForge's decision to entrust spacecraft command to AI represents more than just a technological upgrade - it's a fundamental shift toward truly autonomous space exploration. If Autonomy-1 succeeds, we could be looking at the dawn of an era where AI-powered spacecraft operate as independent explorers, making discoveries and decisions millions of miles from human oversight. The success of this mission won't just validate AstroForge's approach; it could establish the template for how humanity explores the solar system in the decades ahead.

extraction.body: Do Trump's task force and a special envoy for artificial intelligence in the US indicate a move toward regulating this disputed technology, particularly vis-a-vis China? Developers warning against their own technologies and a government unwilling to take action — that was the situation in the first half of September amid concerns in the US that AI models were becoming too powerful. Horizon brings together cloud-native development tools, virtual testing environments, and AI-assisted workflows into a unified platform. This helps car makers and automotive suppliers develop and deliver high-quality software at speed and make engineering more productive. As Horizon's lead industry partner, Volvo Cars is migrating its global AAOS software development environment to the Horizon platform. The platform will give its engineers access to faster development workflows, virtual testing environments and AI-assisted software development tools, freeing engineering teams to spend more time building in-car experiences. "We're building some of the most complex products in the world, which requires a development environment built to match," said Gregor Zetsche, Head of Connected Experience at Volvo Cars. "As Horizon's lead industry partner, we can directly solve our toughest engineering challenges and empower our teams to deliver new experiences faster than ever." Volvo Cars is the lead car maker working with Accenture and Google Cloud to bring the Horizon platform to the industry. Insights from this collaboration will help refine the platform and expand its generative AI capabilities for automotive companies and other industrial manufacturers. Modern vehicles increasingly offer digital experiences, such as navigation, media, voice assistants, connected services and over-the-air software updates. sources.title: Building the Future of Software Engineering in Latin America - Cognition
passages: Last week at MASP (Museu de Arte de São Paulo), one of Latin America’s most iconic landmarks, we announced Cognition’s expansion into Latin America in front of leaders from the region’s largest enterprises, governments, and tech companies.
It’s the first public step toward something bigger: building the future of software engineering in the region.
Meeting that demand will take more than hiring more developers.
Companies need a different way to build, modernize, and maintain software.

Latin America has the talent to lead: 15.8 million developers on GitHub, nearly five times as many as in 2020, and the world’s third-largest developer community behind only the United States and India.
The appetite is not just for the latest technology.
Consumers have embraced WhatsApp, digital banking, and new financial products at remarkable speed.
The systems behind those experiences have not kept pace.
A customer in Brazil can pay for lunch by scanning a QR code while the bank processing the transaction still runs on COBOL.
Partners like these taught us what Devin had to be: an AI software engineer that works inside highly regulated global institutions, where millions of people depend on systems that can never go down.

extraction.body: Last week at MASP (Museu de Arte de São Paulo), one of Latin America’s most iconic landmarks, we announced Cognition’s expansion into Latin America in front of leaders from the region’s largest enterprises, governments, and tech companies. It’s the first public step toward something bigger: building the future of software engineering in the region. São Paulo is our starting point, but our ambition is broader: to help Latin American companies build more of the software their businesses and customers need. Latin America is one of the most mobile-first regions in the world. Consumers have embraced WhatsApp, digital banking, and new financial products at remarkable speed. The systems behind those experiences have not kept pace. A customer in Brazil can pay for lunch by scanning a QR code while the bank processing the transaction still runs on COBOL. Meeting that demand will take more than hiring more developers. Companies need a different way to build, modernize, and maintain software. Latin America has the talent to lead: 15.8 million developers on GitHub, nearly five times as many as in 2020, and the world’s third-largest developer community behind only the United States and India. The appetite is not just for the latest technology. It’s to build what comes next. Some of the region’s most demanding engineering teams already build with Devin: banks like Itaú, Nubank, and Santander; consumer leaders like Natura; and fast-growing technology companies like EBANX. The results speak for themselves. Today, more than 75% of Itaú’s technology teams use Devin: documenting 300,000+ repositories, migrating legacy .NET services to Java 6x faster, and resolving roughly 70% of security vulnerabilities automatically. Bank-wide, Itaú has seen a 20-30% increase in engineering throughput. At Nubank, Latin America’s largest digital bank with roughly 140 million customers, Devin took a multi-million-line monolith migration from years to weeks, at over 20x lower cost. Partners like these taught us what Devin had to be: an AI software engineer that works inside highly regulated global institutions, where millions of people depend on systems that can never go down. The fact that Latin America’s largest companies are moving first on Devin is proof of a pattern we’re seeing everywhere: the enterprises with the most complex, highest-stakes codebases are moving fastest to make autonomous engineering part of how they build software. We hope the results we already have here will push more local banks, telcos, retailers, and governments across the region to ask themselves: why keep importing software built somewhere else, when Latin America has the developers, the market, and now the tooling to build it here first? Our São Paulo team will work with customers across the region, invest in the local developer ecosystem, and help companies build the future of software in Latin America.

extraction.body: Last week at MASP (Museu de Arte de São Paulo), one of Latin America’s most iconic landmarks, we announced Cognition’s expansion into Latin America in front of leaders from the region’s largest enterprises, governments, and tech companies. It’s the first public step toward something bigger: building the future of software engineering in the region. São Paulo is our starting point, but our ambition is broader: to help Latin American companies build more of the software their businesses and customers need. Latin America is one of the most mobile-first regions in the world. Consumers have embraced WhatsApp, digital banking, and new financial products at remarkable speed. The systems behind those experiences have not kept pace. A customer in Brazil can pay for lunch by scanning a QR code while the bank processing the transaction still runs on COBOL. Meeting that demand will take more than hiring more developers. Companies need a different way to build, modernize, and maintain software. Latin America has the talent to lead: 15.8 million developers on GitHub, nearly five times as many as in 2020, and the world’s third-largest developer community behind only the United States and India. The appetite is not just for the latest technology. It’s to build what comes next. Some of the region’s most demanding engineering teams already build with Devin: banks like Itaú, Nubank, and Santander; consumer leaders like Natura; and fast-growing technology companies like EBANX. The results speak for themselves. Today, more than 75% of Itaú’s technology teams use Devin: documenting 300,000+ repositories, migrating legacy .NET services to Java 6x faster, and resolving roughly 70% of security vulnerabilities automatically. Bank-wide, Itaú has seen a 20-30% increase in engineering throughput. At Nubank, Latin America’s largest digital bank with roughly 140 million customers, Devin took a multi-million-line monolith migration from years to weeks, at over 20x lower cost. Partners like these taught us what Devin had to be: an AI software engineer that works inside highly regulated global institutions, where millions of people depend on systems that can never go down. The fact that Latin America’s largest companies are moving first on Devin is proof of a pattern we’re seeing everywhere: the enterprises with the most complex, highest-stakes codebases are moving fastest to make autonomous engineering part of how they build software. We hope the results we already have here will push more local banks, telcos, retailers, and governments across the region to ask themselves: why keep importing software built somewhere else, when Latin America has the developers, the market, and now the tooling to build it here first? Our São Paulo team will work with customers across the region, invest in the local developer ecosystem, and help companies build the future of software in Latin America.

Users can pick from multiple languages broken up into short lessons. When you sign up for either service, the app asks you why you want to learn the new language and what level you’re starting at. Ultimately, you don’t have to choose between the two. Try them both out for free. So the question is — which one to try first? Best for a more traditional learning experience If you want to try something new, Duolingo offers a free course in High Valyrian, the language spoken on Game of Thrones. As a regular Duolingo user, I enjoy the app’s simple, colorful interface and short, gamelike exercises . The app doesn’t restrict how many languages you can try to learn at the same time (personally, I think two is a good maximum if you want to retain anything), or how many lessons you can complete in one day, even on the free version. I use Duolingo to keep up with Spanish and German. It’s an easy app to test the metaphorical waters because it doesn’t require you to create an account right away. For example, even if you start with little to no understanding of Spanish, the lessons are pretty gentle. You’ll choose which picture — paired with the Spanish translation — accurately describes basic phrases and words. Duolingo translates from English to Spanish and back again. Most questions let you tap or click on the Spanish word to translate it in case you get stuck. The app offers additional learning resources if you click the lightbulb icon, as well as the ability to fast-track your lessons if you click the key icon. Duolingo’s “streak” feature motivates you to keep up with your language learning efforts by tracking the number of days you’ve reached your point goal. It can also make it feel like your world is crashing in if you lose an 80-day streak (not that I’m speaking from experience). Resources such as Duolingo Stories, which are short audio stories that allow you to check your comprehension skills as you go, are available online and in the apps. Duolingo also has a podcast that reiterates the lessons you’ve completed. You can subscribe to the premium Duolingo Plus for $10/month for a one-month membership, $8/month for six months, or $7/month for 12 months. Premium gives you ad-free and offline access to the app or website, and the ability to repair a lost streak once a month. You can also access an experimental feature that lets you chat with a language tutor from a country where the language is spoken. This isn’t available for all Duolingo Plus subscribers, though. The Drops app’s fun, colorful layout definitely makes the language you’re trying to learn feel less intimidating, even if you have no prior experience with it. For example, when learning Spanish, the app shows users each word in Spanish and in English, pronounces the word and shows an image of it. Drops’ 5-minute lessons teach vocabulary and phrases by matching images with their corresponding word and vice versa. Despite the repetition of phrases and simple layout, the use of minimalist graphics made me slow down and think each translation through. However, recognizing an image as “to serve” or “excuse me,” instead of “bread” or “fruit” isn’t as easy. There was also a weird hiccup where “el coco” or “the coconut” would trigger Google Assistant on my Pixel 3. I think it’s also advantageous to match the Spanish phrase with an image, instead of with its English translation, as Duolingo does in some lessons. I think this makes it more likely that you’ll associate the image with its Spanish word going forward. The quick, gamelike lessons include word search, swipe style and spelling games. If you get stuck, just tap and hold on the image to get the translation. The overall design and gamification elements make Drops one of the most unique language learning apps I’ve tried so far. Though the main Language Drops lessons aren’t available for PC version yet, the app and mobile browser version do offer Word Drops, which is a supplementary bilingual dictionary for PC, iOS and Android. The service also offers the Scripts app, which teaches the Korean, Japanese, Chinese, Russian and Latin alphabets in Drops style. The Scripts app is a new way to learn a different language’s alphabet. When you create an account, you can try out Drops’ premium features free for seven days. The app offers three different packages — $10/month for a monthly package, $3/month for a yearly package, or a one-time payment of $160 for lifetime access to the app. A premium subscription is ad-free, and offers unlimited lessons, as well as offline access, the ability to restart lessons. If you don’t subscribe to premium, after one lesson, you have to wait until the next day to access another lesson, but you can check out your statistics after completing the lesson (correct answers, wrong answers and words learned) and tap on the words you’ve learned to hear them pronounced again (and see them written with the proper accent marks, etc.). This can give you a leg up when your next lesson starts. If you’re invested in learning a language, I think Drops’ premium features are worth the purchase. For example, I noticed that when the app started incorporating action phrases, like “I serve,” the actions matched with the vocabulary I was learning, so I could more easily learn to construct my own sentences. It’s a bit more challenging than Duolingo, but somehow it feels like I’m learning faster. Both Drops and Duolingo are solid options for those interested in learning a new language (I also liked them both more than Rosetta Stone's more traditional approach ). If game-based learning is your thing, I’d try Drops first. The app’s dragging, tapping and swiping features also feel more intuitive to how we use our phones daily. Drops’ yearly subscription is also only $3/month, compared to Duolingo’s $7/month. However, Duolingo’s free version is a strong option for unlimited language lessons that keep you motivated to keep going. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

extraction.body: Get unlimited access to everything VICE has to offer. I’ve tested most of the language learning apps out there. Here are the ones that work, and the ones you should skip. Not to discourage you, but you’re in for a long haul. Nobody sprints their way to learning a language. Some days you just won’t feel like doing your lesson, and that’s when you begin to lose momentum. I’ve found it’s not the length of time you spend on each lesson, but how regularly you do them. So it’s crucial to your success to find a language-learning app that engages you rather than bores the hell out of you. Luckily for you, there are tons of apps with a bunch of different approaches, so finding one that’s the right fit is easier than it’s ever been. I’ve tried most of the major ones out there. Here are the ones that are worth your time and money (and the ones that aren’t). No app taught me as well as Pimsleur . Even though it’s an app, the core of its teaching goes back decades to before apps even existed. Each audio lesson lasts for 30 minutes and involves listening to and repeating sentences. You don’t get graded or have to select anything on the screen, just correctly say the phrases prompted by the narrator. Because I could hit the play button and then not have to look at my phone for 30 minutes, I’d put on lessons while doing chores around the apartment. They’re structured to repeat bits of previous lessons frequently through subsequent ones, which did a fantastic job of driving them into my long-term memory. Years ago when I first stumbled across this novel app, it wasn’t a guide or a recommendation from a local friend who clued me into iTalki . It was the app’s strong international user base gushing about it on a forum. ITalki works differently than most language apps. Rather than lobbing a bunch of standardized course lessons at you, iTalki has you practice with real people. There are two paths. The first is a free method that acts as a matchmaking service for you and somebody either learning a language you know or who knows a language you’re learning; ideally, both. Then you simply chat. In my experience the switch-off from teaching my language to them teaching me theirs was seamless and natural, and the conversations were actually interesting because we were two real people. No stilted sentences about where to find the nearest hotel. The other path is buying credits to hire a tutor who instructs you over video. The quality varies widely, and the lessons are completely at the tutor’s discretion. Most I saw had degrees from respected institutions and were responsive to queries, and some even offered discounted or free trials before committing. Does the idea of speaking over video to a hired tutor terrify you, or the scheduled lessons that comes with that feels suffocating, but you still like the idea of learning by watching and hearing real people speak real sentences with a natural cadence? Same. Most language apps include sample sentences in over-enunciated, slower-than-normal spoken sentences that bear little resemblance to the way people actually speak. Easy to learn, like training wheels on a bike, but I think it gets in the way of being able to understand actual conversations. The core of Memrise’s lessons are videos of sentences spoken by real people, with real accents. You can take the lessons anytime you want, since they’re pre-recorded. In my experience using it for Spanish, a language I know somewhat well, and Russian, a language I barely know, the people on video sound the most natural of all language apps, by far. Too often I find myself able to understand the very slowly spoken language in a learning program and then struggling to follow along when listening to somebody outside the classroom speak that language. Memrise did the best of the apps to smooth over that transition and taught me, from the get-go, to understand these languages the way their native speakers actually speak them. For each app I took lessons in Spanish, a language I’ve been learning for many years and which I consider myself intermediate already. I can get by conversationally, but there’s still plenty left in my language learning journey. And then I’d also pick a language of which I had a very basic knowledge, such as French or Russian. Practicing both on an app let me know when I was receiving bad advice, such as outdated slang or clunky language that nobody uses outside of a classroom, because I’d know better frrom my experience with Spanish. And on the other extreme it’d give me a window into how effective an app was at teaching me a language as a rank beginner, when I had not much prior experience in grammar, syntax, and basic vocabulary. Look, I already know I’m going to catch a lot of shit for not including Duolingo as a favorite app. I’m speaking from a place of experience. I’ve used it extensively. At one point I had a 550-day-ish streak on the paid version of Duolingo, and that doesn’t include the other, shorter streaks broken before and after. I’ve used it for Spanish, Swahili, French, and Russian. It’s a lot of fun, and it has a lot of heart, and it’s amusing, but it functions (at best) as an occasional tool to help you not forget vocabulary words. It never brought me all that much closer to being conversationally adept. I’ve reviewed Preply , Rocket Languages , Babbel , and Rosetta Stone , and while they all worked better for me than Duolingo, each of them has something that holds me back from awarding them a “best of” ribbon. Babbel was the best of the rest. Its lessons were traditional mixes of spoken and written content. Nothing flashy. It worked, but I felt it was outshone by Pimsleur, iTalki, and Memrise when it came to effectiveness in my learning. Preply was tied entirely to finding a single tutor and taking regular video classes with them, sort of like iTalki offers but with no free inter-community way to practice languages with your peers and less ability to swap instructors. But if you’ve given it a couple of weeks and feel like you haven’t learned at all, then maybe that app just isn’t for you. Try another app. Maybe Rosetta Stone’s “learn like a child” process doesn’t work for you, and perhaps you’ll find that Pimsleur’s audio lessons lead you to retain information in the long-term more effectively. Fluency is the yardstick that many use to measure their language-learning goals, but I’d say achieving a conversational level of a language is a more useful and measurable goal. I’d say that when I hear people talk about fluency, it becomes something so ill-defined and elusive, not just to achieve but to define, that it leads to a lot of unnecessary angst. Can you be fluent if you don’t understand the slang just right, knowing when not to use an outdated saying, and how to deploy the right idioms and obscure vocabulary words rarely used but understood by native speakers? Forget it. If you can understand the language’s jokes, rarely (but not never) have to look up a word, and can both understand real spoken conversations and make yourself broadly understood when you speak, then you can confidently say you’ve learned the language. Any kind of instruction, be it an app, computer program, book, or in-person tutor, is only one tool in the language-learning toolbox. You shouldn’t omit it, but you also shouldn’t expect it to be your only tool. I find that these types of resources are crucial for laying down a foundation of basic, frequently used vocabulary words, as well as an understanding of syntax and grammar. Once you’re more intermediate in your lessons, begin to mix in movies and TV shows in your target language with the subtitles on, listening to songs in your target language and dissecting the lyrics, reading books and the news in your new language, and striking up basic conversations with people. Trying to do these things too early will just result in frustration, but don’t fail to take advantage of them once you have the language’s foundational basics. Keep doing your lessons as you continue to mix in these new resources, too, because they complement each other. This is one big variable built in a laboratory out of many lesser variables. How long it takes for you to become conversational in a language depends on many, many things: your native language, your target language and how dissimilar it is to the languages you already speak well, the amount of time you spend learning each day (longer than an hour per day and the benefits diminish sharply, in my experience), your regularity in practicing (much more important than the amount of time per practice session, again in my experience), and how motivated you are to learn. Learning a language is hard. If it weren’t, then it wouldn’t be an $85 billion industry . Anyone who’s serious about achieving a conversational level in any language, no matter how similar it is to their native language, needs to make a commitment. Take it from me: It sucks when you pour a ton of time into a method, only to learn that it’s not clicking for you and that you’ve wasted your time. I’m not a huge fan of most language apps, but with these we’ve tested here you should be able to find the one that clicks for you. (Honestly, just go with Pimsleur , trust me.) From there, you just have to stick with it, day in and day out. Fifteen minutes a day, every day, is far more effective than an hour done every few days. I’ve tested most of the language learning apps out there. Here are the ones that work, and the ones you should skip.
Not to discourage you, but you’re in for a long haul. Nobody sprints their way to learning a language.

Some days you just won’t feel like doing your lesson, and that’s when you begin to lose momentum. I’ve found it’s not the length of time you spend on each lesson, but how regularly you do them. So it’s crucial to your success to find a language-learning app that engages you rather than bores the hell out of you.

Luckily for you, there are tons of apps with a bunch of different approaches, so finding one that’s the right fit is easier than it’s ever been. I’ve tried most of the major ones out there. Here are the ones that are worth your time and money (and the ones that aren’t).

No app taught me as well as Pimsleur . Even though it’s an app, the core of its teaching goes back decades to before apps even existed. Each audio lesson lasts for 30 minutes and involves listening to and repeating sentences. You don’t get graded or have to select anything on the screen, just correctly say the phrases prompted by the narrator.

Because I could hit the play button and then not have to look at my phone for 30 minutes, I’d put on lessons while doing chores around the apartment. They’re structured to repeat bits of previous lessons frequently through subsequent ones, which did a fantastic job of driving them into my long-term memory.

Years ago when I first stumbled across this novel app, it wasn’t a guide or a recommendation from a local friend who clued me into iTalki . It was the app’s strong international user base gushing about it on a forum. ITalki works differently than most language apps. Rather than lobbing a bunch of standardized course lessons at you, iTalki has you practice with real people.

There are two paths. The first is a free method that acts as a matchmaking service for you and somebody either learning a language you know or who knows a language you’re learning; ideally, both. Then you simply chat. In my experience the switch-off from teaching my language to them teaching me theirs was seamless and natural, and the conversations were actually interesting because we were two real people. No stilted sentences about where to find the nearest hotel.

The other path is buying credits to hire a tutor who instructs you over video. The quality varies widely, and the lessons are completely at the tutor’s discretion. Most I saw had degrees from respected institutions and were responsive to queries, and some even offered discounted or free trials before committing.

Does the idea of speaking over video to a hired tutor terrify you, or the scheduled lessons that comes with that feels suffocating, but you still like the idea of learning by watching and hearing real people speak real sentences with a natural cadence? Same. Most language apps include sample sentences in over-enunciated, slower-than-normal spoken sentences that bear little resemblance to the way people actually speak. Easy to learn, like training wheels on a bike, but I think it gets in the way of being able to understand actual conversations.

The core of Memrise’s lessons are videos of sentences spoken by real people, with real accents. You can take the lessons anytime you want, since they’re pre-recorded. In my experience using it for Spanish, a language I know somewhat well, and Russian, a language I barely know, the people on video sound the most natural of all language apps, by far.

Too often I find myself able to understand the very slowly spoken language in a learning program and then struggling to follow along when listening to somebody outside the classroom speak that language. Memrise did the best of the apps to smooth over that transition and taught me, from the get-go, to understand these languages the way their native speakers actually speak them.

For each app I took lessons in Spanish, a language I’ve been learning for many years and which I consider myself intermediate already. I can get by conversationally, but there’s still plenty left in my language learning journey.

And then I’d also pick a language of which I had a very basic knowledge, such as French or Russian. Practicing both on an app let me know when I was receiving bad advice, such as outdated slang or clunky language that nobody uses outside of a classroom, because I’d know better frrom my experience with Spanish.

And on the other extreme it’d give me a window into how effective an app was at teaching me a language as a rank beginner, when I had not much prior experience in grammar, syntax, and basic vocabulary.

Look, I already know I’m going to catch a lot of shit for not including Duolingo as a favorite app. I’m speaking from a place of experience. I’ve used it extensively. At one point I had a 550-day-ish streak on the paid version of Duolingo, and that doesn’t include the other, shorter streaks broken before and after. I’ve used it for Spanish, Swahili, French, and Russian. It’s a lot of fun, and it has a lot of heart, and it’s amusing, but it functions (at best) as an occasional tool to help you not forget vocabulary words. It never brought me all that much closer to being conversationally adept.

I’ve reviewed Preply , Rocket Languages , Babbel , and Rosetta Stone , and while they all worked better for me than Duolingo, each of them has something that holds me back from awarding them a “best of” ribbon.

Babbel was the best of the rest. Its lessons were traditional mixes of spoken and written content. Nothing flashy. It worked, but I felt it was outshone by Pimsleur, iTalki, and Memrise when it came to effectiveness in my learning.

Preply was tied entirely to finding a single tutor and taking regular video classes with them, sort of like iTalki offers but with no free inter-community way to practice languages with your peers and less ability to swap instructors.

But if you’ve given it a couple of weeks and feel like you haven’t learned at all, then maybe that app just isn’t for you. Try another app. Maybe Rosetta Stone’s “learn like a child” process doesn’t work for you, and perhaps you’ll find that Pimsleur’s audio lessons lead you to retain information in the long-term more effectively.

Fluency is the yardstick that many use to measure their language-learning goals, but I’d say achieving a conversational level of a language is a more useful and measurable goal. I’d say that when I hear people talk about fluency, it becomes something so ill-defined and elusive, not just to achieve but to define, that it leads to a lot of unnecessary angst.

Can you be fluent if you don’t understand the slang just right, knowing when not to use an outdated saying, and how to deploy the right idioms and obscure vocabulary words rarely used but understood by native speakers? Forget it. If you can understand the language’s jokes, rarely (but not never) have to look up a word, and can both understand real spoken conversations and make yourself broadly understood when you speak, then you can confidently say you’ve learned the language.

Any kind of instruction, be it an app, computer program, book, or in-person tutor, is only one tool in the language-learning toolbox. You shouldn’t omit it, but you also shouldn’t expect it to be your only tool. I find that these types of resources are crucial for laying down a foundation of basic, frequently used vocabulary words, as well as an understanding of syntax and grammar.

Once you’re more intermediate in your lessons, begin to mix in movies and TV shows in your target language with the subtitles on, listening to songs in your target language and dissecting the lyrics, reading books and the news in your new language, and striking up basic conversations with people.

Trying to do these things too early will just result in frustration, but don’t fail to take advantage of them once you have the language’s foundational basics. Keep doing your lessons as you continue to mix in these new resources, too, because they complement each other.

This is one big variable built in a laboratory out of many lesser variables. How long it takes for you to become conversational in a language depends on many, many things: your native language, your target language and how dissimilar it is to the languages you already speak well, the amount of time you spend learning each day (longer than an hour per day and the benefits diminish sharply, in my experience), your regularity in practicing (much more important than the amount of time per practice session, again in my experience), and how motivated you are to learn.

Learning a language is hard. If it weren’t, then it wouldn’t be an $85 billion industry . Anyone who’s serious about achieving a conversational level in any language, no matter how similar it is to their native language, needs to make a commitment.

Take it from me: It sucks when you pour a ton of time into a method, only to learn that it’s not clicking for you and that you’ve wasted your time. I’m not a huge fan of most language apps, but with these we’ve tested here you should be able to find the one that clicks for you. (Honestly, just go with Pimsleur , trust me.)
From there, you just have to stick with it, day in and day out. Fifteen minutes a day, every day, is far more effective than an hour done every few days.
